title: The Long Boom and the Cheap-Oil Twilight: A World History, 2025–2065
body:
The second quarter of the twenty-first century began unsteadily. In 2026 a coup struck Canada, of all places. The Sahel kept producing coups, as did Sudan, Haiti and Myanmar. World output per person rose slowly, from about $18,300 to nearly $20,000 by 2030. That year Malaysia and Singapore went to war, and Russia and the United States entered a confrontation of their own. Greece fell to a coup the same year, and internal fighting broke out across Latin America, from Mexico to Colombia.

The defining shock came in 2033. The oil index jumped from 119 to 362 and peaked at 466 in 2035. Importers were squeezed hard, and growth stalled for several years. During those lean years Sri Lanka fought Russia (2035), civil conflict reached the United States and France, and in 2039 the great rivalry turned into open war between China and the United States. India and Pakistan, and China and India, also clashed repeatedly.

Then, against expectations, prosperity arrived. Oil prices eased, and from 2041 to 2045 world income per person jumped from about $24,900 to $32,900, the fastest climb of the era. A pandemic in 2046 stopped the surge, but it did not reverse it. Meanwhile, war spread more widely: the share of nations in conflict reached its highest point, about 23 percent, around 2050. Armenia and Azerbaijan fought in 2049, and Gambia and Senegal in 2056. Portugal and Germany suffered repeated slumps, and Hong Kong suffered a long stagnation.

By the 2050s oil had fallen to a quarter of its 2024 price. Producers like Angola, Kazakhstan and Gabon slumped together. World income peaked near $38,900 in 2059. India and Pakistan went to war again in 2060, and income then slid to about $34,200 by 2065. Even so, by then conflict had receded to its lowest level of the forty years. The world was richer and calmer, but no longer growing.

title: The Long Quieting: A World History, 2025–2065
body:
The era opened badly. In 2026 a fifth of the world's nations were living with armed conflict, and new internal conflicts broke out in places as unlike one another as Burundi, Russia and the United States. The Middle East took the worst of the next decade: wars between Iraq and Syria and between Israel and Jordan in 2028, Iraq against Kuwait in 2029, and Iran against Israel in 2032. Through the whole period, coups came again and again to Central Africa and the Sahel, above all in the Democratic Republic of Congo, Cameroon, Chad and Sudan.

Oil changed the story twice. Prices collapsed after 2030, and by 2035 the oil index stood at 60. That was ruinous for petro-states like Qatar and a gift to importers. Then prices reversed. A spike in 2036 coincided with a slump in China and the first fall in world output of the era. The real shock came in 2043, when the index reached 333, more than three times its 2024 level. Remarkably, the world economy kept growing through it, and over the next twenty years oil drifted back to about where it began.

The great powers did not stay at peace. China fought Vietnam in 2038 and India in 2047, and again in 2056. Iran fought Pakistan in 2047, and the two Koreas went to war in 2057. In 2050 a broad recession reached more than thirty countries at once, with Africa, Eastern Europe and Latin America hit hardest. Yet the share of nations in conflict kept shrinking, and by 2052 it was below one percent.

By 2065 the average person was more than twice as rich as in 2025, at roughly $39,000 a head. Egypt and China had seen repeated democratic gains. Even so, the closing year brought six coups and fresh disputes between Oman and Saudi Arabia, a reminder that calm is never a final state.

title: The Long Fever: A World History, 2025–2065
body:
The era began with the great powers at war. In 2026 China and the United Kingdom went to war, and in 2032 China fought India. For eight years the world economy went nowhere. Output per person hovered around $17,000 and dipped twice, while the United States slumped almost every year. In 2029 civil conflict broke out inside America itself. Elsewhere the old fault lines gave way: Eritrea fought Ethiopia in 2028, Iran fought Oman in 2033, and a scattering of coups ran across the Sahel and the Horn. Madagascar overthrew its rulers again and again.

Recovery came suddenly in 2034. Over the next decade output per person rose past $22,000, even as the world grew more violent. By 2045–46 more than a quarter of all countries were at war with themselves, the highest share of the era, and a second civil conflict broke out in the United States. Oil collapsed to an index of 29 in 2041, which ruined producers. A pandemic followed in 2042. The wars moved toward South Asia and Africa: Bangladesh fought India in 2041, Ethiopia fought Sudan in 2044, and Myanmar fought Pakistan in 2047.

The great shock came in 2053. Oil prices nearly tripled that year and passed eleven times their 2024 level by 2055. Growth stalled for three years. That same year, 2053, war broke out between Germany and Ireland, and Germany went on to fight the Netherlands in 2059. China fought Kazakhstan in 2057, and India and Pakistan returned to war in 2060. Strangely, internal conflict eased during the oil crisis and fell to its lowest level of the era.

By 2065 oil had returned to normal, and output per person had nearly doubled to about $34,000. In 2064 dozens of countries moved toward democracy at once, among them China's neighbours India and Japan. Yet the American republic was weakening, and new rebellions were flaring across Africa. The fever had broken, but it had not gone.

title: The Long Discount: A History of the World, 2025–2065
body:
The decades that followed 2025 opened in turmoil. In 2027 civil strife broke out in the United States and Brazil, and Malaysia and Singapore went to war. India and Pakistan clashed in 2029, the same year unrest reached Taiwan. Coups toppled governments in Myanmar and, startlingly, Iceland. Through all this the world economy kept growing. Output per person rose from about $18,600 to $21,000 by 2029, and oil prices fell after a brief spike in 2027.

From 2030, intellectual work began to cost almost nothing. Uptake was slow at first, and the instability got worse before it eased. By 2033–34 more than a quarter of the world's countries were caught up in conflict, while Mali, Chad and Sudan saw repeated coups. Then oil collapsed. The index fell to 30 in 2036, which hurt producers like Angola and Iraq and eased costs for importers. The United States fought wars against Yemen in 2037 and Romania in 2038, and its democracy weakened several times over these years.

The reckoning came in the Great Slump of 2041–43, when about half the world was using the new machines. World output per person fell from $33,000 to $30,500. In 2042 more than fifty economies contracted at once, from Canada and Russia to most of Africa. Democracy slipped across Europe, from Belgium to Bulgaria to Japan. Afghanistan and Pakistan went to war in 2044.

Recovery, once it came, was dramatic. By 2056 the machines were everywhere, and world output per person doubled in two decades to $80,000 by 2065. Old flashpoints still flared: Spain had a coup in 2047, and China and Taiwan went to war in 2055. Even so, the share of countries in conflict fell to a historic low of 9 percent. In 2059 about thirty nations moved toward democracy at once. The era nonetheless ended uneasily. In 2065 a pandemic struck, and new wars broke out between Montenegro and Slovakia and between the United States and Uzbekistan.
